audience.programmeDescription: Artificial Intelligence at the University of Groningen combines computing and mathematics with the study of mind, brain and language. This example follows Computational Neuroscience and concludes with a research project.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The closest UCR option combines AI, cognition and robotics. The other options emphasise computational methods or the science of human cognition. Groningen has separate courses in natural language processing and brain modelling.

componentNotes.y1-fundamentals: Groningen brings reasoning, agents, perception and language processing together in one course.
componentNotes.y1-intro-ai: Groningen gives students a separate overview of AI as a field.
componentNotes.y2-advanced-logic: Groningen continues formal logic in a separate course.
componentNotes.y2-applied-ml: Groningen requires a project that takes machine learning from data preparation to model evaluation. UCR applies machine learning in several courses.
componentNotes.y2-architectures: Groningen uses computational architectures to model human cognition.
componentNotes.y1-linguistics: Groningen teaches general linguistics. UCR’s Psycholinguistics course focuses on how people process language.
componentNotes.y2-nlp: Groningen teaches computational processing of text and language. UCR’s Psycholinguistics course focuses on human language processing.
componentNotes.y3-cognitive-neuroscience: The regulations list this course from 2027–2028. UCR studies cognition and its neural basis in several courses.
componentNotes.y3-brain-modelling: Groningen uses computational tools to model mechanisms of the brain.
componentNotes.y3-neural: Groningen studies computation inspired by neural circuits. UCR’s neural networks course focuses on deep learning.
componentNotes.y2-skills: Groningen has a separate scientific skills course. UCR develops research methods across its curriculum.
componentNotes.y3-project: Groningen requires an AI research project. Independent research at UCR is optional.
componentNotes.y3-minor: Students complete a 30 EC minor or other approved study.

ACCPPDE101.name: Personal & Professional Development
ACCPPDE101.text: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.

BENBUSI211.name: Business & Economy in the Age of AI
BENBUSI211.text: Examines AI's business, economic and societal implications without requiring a technical background. Students study AI's capabilities and limits, applications across business functions and industries, and effects on labour markets, productivity, innovation and inequality. Business cases and scholarly arguments support analysis of governance, regulation and a country's AI readiness and industrial policy.

DISARIN111.name: AI Ethics
DISARIN111.text: AI Ethics examines artificial intelligence from philosophical and psychological perspectives. Topics include fairness, privacy, responsibility, human-value alignment, moral status and political or existential risks. Students apply ethical frameworks to questions about human behaviour and interaction, synthesise research in an analytical psychology project, and produce a research-based podcast.

DISARIN211.name: Decision-making in AI
DISARIN211.text: Decision-making in AI examines how intelligent agents make decisions under uncertainty. Students study probability, Bayesian networks, temporal models, expected utility, Markov decision processes, partial observability and bandit problems. Multi-agent decisions and probabilistic programming extend the analysis, supported by equations, numerical examples and scientific papers.

DISARIN212.name: Logic & Discrete Mathematics
DISARIN212.text: Introduces formal logic, abstract reasoning and proof. Students work with propositions, quantified statements, sets, Boolean algebra, functions and relations, direct and indirect proofs, induction and recursion. A final component models processes and games without chance and investigates winning strategies.

DISARIN311.text: Optimization Methods in AI studies search and optimisation for rational agents. Topics include uninformed and heuristic search, local and global optimisation, adversarial search, constraint satisfaction, linear programming and discrete optimisation. Laboratory exercises and projects develop algorithm implementation, evaluation and experimental investigation of small intelligent systems.

HCBCOGN311.name: Higher Order Functions
HCBCOGN311.text: Higher Order Functions deepens knowledge of neurophysiology, neuroanatomy and experimental cognitive neuroscience. Topics include attention, memory, emotion, cognitive control, social cognition, pain and consciousness. An attentional-blink experiment and a team research proposal develop engagement with empirical research, experimental design and ethical reflection.

HCBCOGN312.name: Psycholinguistics
HCBCOGN312.text: Psycholinguistics is the study of the neurobiological and psychological factors that enable us to acquire, use, and understand language. Modern research draws on cognitive psychology, neuroscience, and computer science to investigate how language is processed. The course focuses primarily, though not exclusively, on the neuroscience of language. Students examine theoretical and experimental issues in speech production and comprehension, language impairments, the relationship between thought and language, and the evolution and acquisition of language. They also gain hands-on experience with experimental approaches to the study of language and develop an understanding of human linguistic capacity as a subject of multidisciplinary research. Topics covered: What is language? Evolutionary aspects of language and animal communication; language and thought; aphasia; language acquisition; bilingualism; speech comprehension; semantics; reading and dyslexia; speech production.
